{{Short description|Cone of outward normals to a convex set at a point}}

In [[convex analysis]] and [[optimization (mathematics)|optimization]], the '''normal cone''' to a set at a point is a [[convex cone]] consisting of vectors that make a non-acute angle with every feasible direction from the point. For a [[convex set]], it is the [[Dual cone and polar cone|polar cone]] of the [[tangent cone]] and gives a geometric form of first-order optimality conditions.{{sfn|Rockafellar|1970|§23}}{{sfn|Rockafellar|Wets|1998|Ch. 6}}

== Definition ==

Let <math>C</math> be a convex subset of a finite-dimensional real inner product space <math>V</math>, and let <math>x\in C</math>. The '''normal cone''' to <math>C</math> at <math>x</math> is

<math display="block">
N_C(x)=\{v\in V:\langle v,y-x\rangle\leq 0\text{ for all }y\in C\}.
</math>

If <math>x\notin C</math>, the normal cone is often defined to be empty. The elements of <math>N_C(x)</math> are called [[normal vector]]s to <math>C</math> at <math>x</math>. The sign convention above gives outward normals.

If <math>x</math> is an interior point of <math>C</math>, then <math>N_C(x)=\{0\}</math>. If <math>C</math> is a smooth full-dimensional convex body and <math>x</math> is a boundary point, then <math>N_C(x)</math> is the ray generated by the outward normal vector at <math>x</math>.

== Subgradients ==

Normal cones are closely related to [[subgradient]]s. If <math>f:V\to\mathbb R\cup\{+\infty\}</math> is a proper [[convex function]], then its [[epigraph]]
<math display="block">\operatorname{epi} f=\{(x,t):t\geq f(x)\}</math>
is a convex set. A vector <math>p\in V</math> is a subgradient of <math>f</math> at <math>x</math> if and only if{{sfn|Rockafellar|1970|§23}}{{sfn|Borwein|Lewis|2006|Ch 3}}
<math display="block">(p,-1)\in N_{\operatorname{epi} f}(x,f(x)).</math>

Equivalently,
<math display="block">f(y)\geq f(x)+\langle p,y-x\rangle\quad\text{for all }y.</math>

=== Sublevel sets ===
Still with <math>f</math> a proper convex function, consider the [[sublevel set]] through a point <math>x</math>:
<math display="block">C=\{y:f(y)\leq f(x)\}.</math>
Every subgradient of
<math>f</math> at <math>x</math> determines a normal vector to <math>C</math> at
<math>x</math>. Indeed, if <math>p\in\partial f(x)</math> and <math>y\in C</math>, then
<math display="block">\langle p,y-x\rangle\leq f(y)-f(x)\leq 0.</math>

Under standard regularity hypotheses, for example when
<math>x\in\operatorname{core}(\operatorname{dom} f)</math> and <math>x</math> is not a
minimizer of <math>f</math>, the converse also holds:
<math display="block">N_C(x)=\mathbb R_+\,\partial f(x),</math>
or equivalently the normal cone to the sublevel set is the closed convex cone
generated by the subdifferential.{{sfn|Rockafellar|1970|§23}}{{sfn|Borwein|Lewis|2006|Ch. 3}}
